strengths: Proposes a novel 'iterative paradigm' for story visualization that is conceptually distinct from existing Auto-Regressive and Reference-Image paradigms, using all previously generated images as evolving global references rather than fixed or local ones, which plausibly reduces error accumulation and propagation of reference-image flaws.

The proposed Global Reference Cross-Attention (GRCA) module is training-free and plug-and-play, reusing pretrained cross-attention weights, and is shown to scale much better in FLOPs than Consistent Self-Attention (CSA) as the number of reference images grows.

Extensive empirical evaluation across regular-length (StorySalon) and long-story (up to 100 frames) settings, with quantitative metrics (CLIP-T, aCCS, aFID), qualitative comparisons, ablations on initialization/GRCA/iteration schedule, and human evaluation, plus an additional comparison against subject-consistent generation baselines (IP-Adapter, PhotoMaker, StoryDiffusion).
Reasonably comprehensive appendix with additional analyses (effect of number of iterations, different visual styles, more qualitative examples) that supports the paper's central claims.
Clear visual evidence (e.g., Fig. 1, 4, 5, 7) that the method better preserves fine-grained interactions and subject identity compared to StoryDiffusion and StoryGen in several showcased examples.
weaknesses: The iterative paradigm requires L=10 full diffusion passes (each with 50 DDIM steps) over the entire story to refine all frames, which represents a substantial multiplicative increase in wall-clock generation cost compared to single-pass baselines (StoryDiffusion, StoryGen); the paper's efficiency claims and FLOPs comparisons (Fig. 8) only address per-image attention cost with varying numbers of references, not the total end-to-end computational/time budget across iterations, leaving the actual efficiency trade-off unclear or potentially unfavorable.

Table 6 reports aFID with an upward arrow (↑) while aFID is defined as Fréchet Inception Distance elsewhere in the paper with a downward-better convention (↓); this inconsistency is confusing and raises questions about whether the metric or its interpretation is correctly reported, undermining confidence in the reported ablation trends.

For the long-story setting, stories and descriptions are synthesized via GPT-4o without real ground-truth images, making it unclear how aFID/aCCS are computed (i.e., what serves as the reference distribution), which raises reproducibility and validity concerns for this core evaluation.

The linear weighting schedule for λ (0.3 to 0.5) and the choice of 10 iterations appear to be tuned heuristically based on the same benchmarks used for evaluation, with limited principled justification or sensitivity analysis beyond a coarse ablation.

Comparisons are largely restricted to a small set of relatively recent but not exhaustive baselines (StoryGen, StoryDiffusion, AR-LDM, IP-Adapter, PhotoMaker); several other recent story-visualization methods discussed in the related work (e.g., StoryImager, AutoStory, TheaterGen) are not included in the quantitative comparison, weakening claims of state-of-the-art superiority.

Human evaluation protocol details (number of participants, inter-rater agreement, statistical significance) are not reported, limiting the ability to assess the robustness of the reported preference scores.
Minor presentation issues, such as a placeholder 'https URL' in the abstract instead of an actual project link, reduce polish and could hint at incomplete preparation for submission.
